claims.claim: The web UI shows a plan as one card (a bar of its steps' states, the steps in the order they can run, Cancel plan and its evidence run), with what each running step's peer is doing now. A team step is labelled as one and shows its lead's team steps live, then the team run it came back with; the lead's page shows the team run as a plan of its own, for the peer whose step it is. The plan editor checks team steps as they are written (team, levels=, timeout=, and the options a team step can't take).

A folder's owner can leave its team plans to their agent's model instead of writing one (proofkin share team NAME --model, optionally --approve; a written plan and the model exclude each other, and peers see either as a folder that takes team steps). For each team step it is handed, the lead's model writes the team plan with the owner's default model and effort for its first provider, read-only in the folder, holding a task slot only while it writes, from a prompt with the task as handed down, how a team plan is written and the team it may use (its peers except the agents the work came from, its squads and skills).       The plan is the answer's first fenced block, checked as an owner's plan is before it runs; one that doesn't check out goes back to the model with what is wrong, up to 3 tries in all, and then fails the step. With --approve the owner approves each plan first: they may ask for changes, at most twice, which the model makes before they are asked again, and a plan they reject fails the step. The team run's plan (in a comment) and the lead's answer say whose model wrote it for whose step, and whether the owner approved it and after how many rounds of changes. A lead that runs no models refuses such team steps.

The web UI lets an owner have a folder's model write its team plans (Team plan…: who writes it, I do or My model writes one for each team step, with Ask me to approve each plan before it runs): PUT /api/shares/NAME/team with {"model": true, "approve": bool} saves it for the running agent and in shares.json, and the reply, the activity and the page's shares (team_model, team_approval) say what the folder does now. A written plan and the model replace each other, DELETE removes either, and a body that says neither or both is refused with what to send, as the data share and a folder it doesn't share are.

With a tracker linked (a repository and, optionally, a GitHub Project), each plan run is tracked on GitHub: the run gets an issue (or works on an existing one with track: #N; track: <title> names a new one and track: off leaves the run untracked) and each step a sub-issue of it (or an existing issue named with issue=#N, made a sub-issue of the run's), assigned to the profile's GitHub account and blocked by the issues of the steps it runs after. On the board each item says which agent does it (an Agent field, added if the board has none).       A later run on the same issue takes up its steps' open sub-issues again, unless a run at the same time works on them: then it makes its own. A sub-issue it takes up gets its step's title and text in that run, and a comment that the run took it over. A plan can't give two steps one issue, or a step the run's own.

The board follows a tracked run: a step's item is In progress while it runs (with the peer doing it, moved once however often the peer reports), In review while its committed work waits for a pull request or its sign-off for a person, and Done once closed; a step that changed no files is closed when it is done; a failed or skipped step goes back to Todo. Each result and failure is commented on its issue with its signed evidence (signer, checks, commit and branch),       and the run's issue gets the verdict and its claims; it is closed once all its sub-issues are, waiting in review while its own steps' pull requests are open (and where it was while other work is), and it goes back to where it was if the run failed. Only an issue a run made (its body has the run marker: track: <title>, or no track: line) is closed, set In review or Done, or left for settling: an issue a person named with track: #N goes back where it was and stays open, and the run's comment says why; settling lets go of one an earlier version left waiting, without closing it. Without the project scope tracking keeps to the issues and says how to grant it, and tracking never fails or holds up the plan's steps.

A tracked step's task carries its issue and those of the steps whose work it applies. The worker's commit references them in Refs: trailers (only well-formed owner/repo#N references, since they come from a peer, as is the subject a step that works on an issue asks for, of which only the first line is used), its task branch lists them, and a pull request opened from the branch (repo pr or the web UI) closes them, so GitHub links the pull request to the issues and closes them when it merges.

A profile links its tracker with its GitHub account (proofkin tracker link, or the web UI's Tracker card), which checks the repository and the board (a project given by its address or owner/number) and shows the board's statuses, or why the board isn't used and the command that fixes it. Every request is GitHub GraphQL through the GitHub CLI, on stdin, with the token only in gh's environment.       The board's items (or the open issues) are listed by status with their agent, assignees, sub-issue progress and closing pull requests, and Plan it starts a plan on an item with a step per open sub-issue; tracker add (or Add existing issues) puts the repository's issues and pull requests on the board with a status from their state (open issues to do, open pull requests in review, closed and merged ones done), keeping statuses already set. Tracked steps, plans and runs link their issues, and the plan editor knows track: and issue=.

The Tracker card, tracker status and tracker sync say what each run issue left open is waiting for: the run's number, title and link, how many of its sub-issues are closed, and each open sub-issue with the pull request that will close it, or that no pull request does yet. They are read in one GraphQL query and returned as waiting by GET /api/tracker and POST /api/tracker/sync, which also returns the run issues it closed. Runs that are closed or gone are left out.

The Work IQ client speaks MCP over streamable HTTP to a configurable endpoint (default https://workiq.svc.cloud.microsoft/mcp). It sends initialize (protocol 2025-06-18, client info proofkin and its version) and then notifications/initialized, keeps the Mcp-Session-Id and sends it with the MCP-Protocol-Version on later requests, and starts a new session once, sending the request again, when a request with a session gets 404. Every request carries Accept, Content-Type, a bearer token from the TokenSource and a new client-request-id in UUID v4 form. JSON and Server-Sent Events replies are both read (the SSE response is the event answering the request, skipping notifications). tools/list is cached per client. A typed call whose tool is missing waits 2 seconds, lists once more and keeps the new list, and gives a clear error if the tool is still missing. Tool listings are not audited or counted against budgets. The request-id, x-ms-request-id, client-request-id and x-ms-correlation-id of a response are kept with the result and with errors. The messages go through a Transport trait so a stdio transport can reuse the client.

Work IQ errors are classified and only the safe ones are retried. A WorkIqError has a class (sign in again, consent, denied by policy, billing, throttled with its delay, transient, uncertain change, other tool error), the request and correlation ids and a fix saying what to do and who can do it, and its message is one line: what happened, the fix, the ids; when a tool reports the failure itself (isError, stoppedReason error), the message keeps what it said, redacted and at most 300 characters. The class comes from the HTTP status (401, 402, 403, 429, 5xx), a WWW-Authenticate invalid_token or insufficient_claims challenge, JSON-RPC errors, tool results with isError, and payloads with stoppedReason error, errorCode, recoveryAction and retryAfterSeconds (under application/vnd.ms-workiq.retrieval and at the top level); AADSTS65001 and consent_required mean consent, AADSTS50105 and AADSTS53003 a denial with the admin's fix, spending policy and billing errors billing. A 401 makes the TokenSource refresh once and the call is sent once more (a failed refresh is reported with its reason). A throttled read waits for Retry-After or retryAfterSeconds when it is at most 60 seconds, at most twice. A transient failure of a read tool (retrieve, ask, fetch, fetch_blob, search_paths, get_schema, list_agents, discover) is retried at most twice with exponential backoff and jitter. Policy denials, consent, billing and every other tool, including the change tools, are never sent again after a failure, and a change that timed out or lost its connection is reported as uncertain. Waiting goes through an injectable Sleeper so tests don't wait.

A profile can have a Work IQ account: ProfileConfig.workiq, left out of profile.json when absent, with the connection (hosted with tenant and client id, or the CLI with an optional tenant), the user (UPN, display name, tenant id) and when it was added. Nothing secret is in profile.json: the refresh token is in the profile's secret store under the key workiq. The token source for a hosted account keeps the access token and its expiry in memory only, and refreshes it at the tenant's Entra token endpoint (grant_type refresh_token, client_id, refresh_token and the WorkIQAgent.Ask offline_access openid profile scope) five minutes before it expires. A new refresh token from Entra is saved and used for the next refresh. Callers at the same moment wait for one refresh, which also holds for the client's 401 refresh. invalid_grant and interaction_required are the sign-in-again class with the fix proofkin auth login workiq --profile P. A digital worker uses its owner's Work IQ account only when the owner turned that on for it (workiq_from_owner, set by proofkin worker create --workiq, which needs the owner signed in to Work IQ); otherwise the error says how. proofkin auth status shows the account, and proofkin auth logout workiq removes the account and its token.

proofkin auth login workiq --tenant T --client-id C [--device-code] --profile P signs a profile in to Work IQ. The browser flow is the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256 over a random verifier, a random state): a loopback listener on 127.0.0.1 with the redirect http://localhost:<port>, the browser opened (through a hook) and the URL printed, the authorize request with response type code, response mode query and the WorkIQAgent.Ask offline_access openid profile scopes and no resource parameter, the state checked (a wrong state is refused and the code is not used), the code exchanged with the verifier, and a page saying the window can be closed. The device code flow with --device-code prints Entra's message and polls the token endpoint at the interval given through authorization_pending and slow_down, and ends on expired_token and authorization_declined. The account (user, name and tenant from the unverified id token) is saved with the refresh token in the secret store, and the sign-in is checked right away with tools/list against Work IQ; if that fails the profile is signed out again. AADSTS65001 and consent_required (with the admin consent URL for the client id and tenant), AADSTS50105, AADSTS700016, AADSTS90002 and AADSTS7000218 are explained in clear words, also when Entra reports them in the browser redirect.

proofkin auth login workiq --cli [--account EMAIL] [--cli-path PATH] --profile P connects a profile to Microsoft's Work IQ CLI, which signs in by itself with its own app and picks the tenant from its account (--tenant is refused with --cli: the CLI has no tenant option): the sign-in finds the CLI (--cli-path, which must exist, else workiq on the PATH, else in npm's global folder from npm prefix -g, which a Node version manager keeps off the PATH) and saves the account (connection kind cli with the account given and where the CLI is) with no token in the secret store; the user shown is the account given, else the one the CLI reports in its initialize reply (serverInfo.user, else serverInfo.upn), else its default account (defaultAccount in workiq config show), else Work IQ CLI, and auth status and the doctor say '<user> through the Work IQ CLI'; the sign-in is checked right away with tools/list through the CLI and signed out again if that fails. A StdioTransport (the client's Transport over a child process) starts the CLI the sign-in found while it is there, else workiq on the PATH, else npx -y @microsoft/workiq, running mcp with --account when the account has one; it writes newline-delimited JSON-RPC to the child's stdin and reads replies line by line from its stdout, skipping notifications and lines that are not JSON and matching responses by id. The MCP client runs initialize, tools/list and tools/call over it. A child that exited is started again once, and gets the initialize handshake again before the message; a change tool that may already have reached a child that crashed is not sent again (reported as uncertain), and a second crash is an error. The child is killed when the transport is dropped. The child gets the agent's environment minus the inherited credential variables the providers' processes lose (GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY and the rest of INHERITED_CREDENTIAL_VARS). A CLI account has no bearer: its token source gives nothing. workiq::connect(profile) builds the client for the profile's account, hosted or CLI, and client_for_profile uses it. When the CLI says its EULA is not accepted (its error mentions the EULA or accept-eula), the error says to run workiq accept-eula yourself and that Proofkin never accepts it for you. If a tool is still missing after listing again, the error says the CLI may still be loading its tools and, if it lists accept_eula, suggests running workiq accept-eula yourself.

proofkin workiq doctor [--json] --profile P (docs/work-iq.md section 10) runs five checks in order against the account the profile uses, through workiq::connect_at, and stops at the first that fails; its address for the discovery document, the MCP endpoint and Entra are configurable (workiq::Endpoints) so tests use fakes. (1) Discovery, hosted accounts only (skipped otherwise): a GET of the protected-resource metadata answers with resource and authorization_servers. (2) Sign-in: the profile has a Work IQ account and, when hosted, its refresh token. (3) Token, hosted only: a fresh access token whose claims, decoded only for this diagnosis, have an aud of api://workiq.svc.cloud.microsoft or fdcc1f02-fc51-4226-8753-f668596af7f7, the account's tid, and WorkIQAgent.Ask in scp. (4) tools/list works and offers retrieve. (5) One small retrieve (query Proofkin connection check), audited with the purpose doctor and counted against the budgets. Each failure says what is wrong, the fix and who makes it, from the client's error classes where they apply: the Work IQ service principal (az ad sp create --id fdcc1f02-fc51-4226-8753-f668596af7f7, a tenant admin), admin consent (the adminconsent URL of the account's client id and tenant), user assignment (an admin, Enterprise applications, Users and groups), billing and the spending policy (a billing admin, Microsoft 365 admin center), the Work IQ MCP policy (an admin, Microsoft 365 admin center, Agents, Tools, Work IQ MCP), or signing in again (the user). --json prints the profile, whether all passed, and each check's name, result (ok, failed or skipped), detail and fix (who and action). The command exits 1 when a check fails. proofkin doctor shows one Work IQ line per profile (signed in or not, and the connection) without network calls.

The Work IQ content policy (src/workiq/content.rs, docs/work-iq.md section 3) reads retrieve results from structuredContent under application/vnd.ms-workiq.retrieval, never from the MCP content array, and fails on isError, stoppedReason error or a missing structuredContent. Only results whose contentProtection is exactly allowed (after trimming) are kept; the rest, a missing value included, are withheld and counted as missing, blocked or other. The one exception is a People result (entityType People) with no contentProtection at all, as Work IQ gives them: a Local audience gets it as if Work IQ had said allowed, with the label it carries (unknown without one, so nothing made from it goes to a peer), and a Peer never does, whatever its label and its grant (unlabeled included): it is withheld and counted as missing. A People result whose contentProtection is blocked or any other value, or null (counted as missing), and any other result without one, are withheld for a Local audience too. The audit's withheld count (summarize) follows the same rules as the prompt section. A Local audience gets every label; a Peer gets only the labels in its allowlist (compared without case), and unlabeled allows results without a label; results withheld by label are counted too. Markdown, titles and links are redacted, a result's title and date come from its resourceMetadata facet (document, email, meeting, chat or web; dates from sentTime, startTime and the Graph date names), results are kept by relevance when Work IQ scores them, else in Work IQ's order, up to a character cap (16000 by default), and each result is wrapped in the external-content envelope, followed by a Sources list (also wrapped) and a line with the withheld counts, under the heading saying the context is cited and unverified. Real results (Work IQ CLI 1.0.1: Files and Emails with a label object, Meetings and Chats without one, People without contentProtection) are read as such: labeled ones keep their displayName, unlabeled ones count as unknown and go to no peer, and People go only to a Local audience. An ask answer is read from structuredContent (answer, text, markdown or response), as Work IQ gives it, else from the result's text content (its response, when that text is the JSON object Work IQ's tool reference documents); its citations come only from structuredContent, and an answer whose citations have no label metadata, or that has none, is local only: a Peer gets nothing from it.

A peer's Microsoft 365 grant (docs/work-iq.md section 4) is the optional m365 field of its entry in peers.json, left out when absent, with labels (the label names it may receive; unlabeled allows content without a label) and tools (its tasks may use this agent's Work IQ gateway, read only). Absent means nothing is allowed. proofkin peers allow <peer> --m365 General,Public,unlabeled [--m365-tools] sets it (names trimmed and without duplicates, through M365Grant::from_labels; unknown, off among label names and no label names are refused in words that name the flag), --m365 off on its own removes it (not with --m365-tools), and running peers allow again without --m365 keeps the current grant; peers list shows it, and the web UI's allowlist shows and sets it too (WIQ-23). The audience for content sent to a peer is Local for the owner's own digital workers, a Peer audience with the grant's labels for a granted peer, and none (refuse) for any other peer.

Microsoft 365 content keeps its origin (docs/work-iq.md section 4) and plans don't send it to peers not allowed to receive it. A knowledge topic with front matter origin: workiq and labels: (comma-separated) is marked (parse_mark, with_mark and KnowledgeBase::marks in src/knowledge.rs); a mark can be written into a topic with or without troubleshooting-guide front matter, a guide stays a guide, and a topic can have both. A step (Step.m365, a field the workiq= option and @workiq steps will set too) is marked when a context= topic is marked, with the union of the labels (context=all included), when a step it runs after is marked because it gets that step's output, and the steps that save= from a marked step write the mark into the topic, so a later step that uses it is marked. The plan check (preflight, with the allowlist and the owner's digital workers as Recipients) gives an error for a marked step whose target (a peer, a squad member the squad may pick, or the person asked to approve) has no Microsoft 365 grant or whose grant lacks one of the labels, naming the step, the peer, the labels and the proofkin peers allow command that grants them; a granted peer (labels compared without case) and the owner's digital workers get none. When the plan runs, the same check is made against the allowlist as it is then before each task is sent, and the step fails with the same message if the grant changed.

Every Work IQ call through Client::call_tool_in (done, failed or refused) appends one JSON line to <profile>/workiq-audit.jsonl (append only, behind a lock, a write error only warns): time, tool, purpose (step with the run id and step, knowledge import, gateway, doctor or command), audience (local or the peer's name), the query's SHA-256 and length and never its text, outcome (ok, refused, or the error class), the results and withheld counts and the labels seen when the result has them, the request, x-ms-request, client-request and correlation ids, and the duration. A status of 400 or more inside any tool answer (including a notice send), given as a number or numeric text, is recorded with its error class instead of ok, even when Work IQ did not flag the call as an error. Answered failures still count against the budgets. Budgets in profile.json (workiq_budget: calls_per_day, default 200; calls_per_run, default 25) are checked before a call is sent: a call over a budget fails with an over-budget error that names the budget and the proofkin workiq budget command that raises it, is not sent, and is audited as refused (refused calls don't count). Usage today and per run is counted from the log, the day being the local date from an injectable clock, so a new day resets the daily count. proofkin workiq usage --profile P prints today's use against the budgets and proofkin workiq budget --per-day N --per-run N --profile P changes them (a limit left out is kept; zero is refused).

The workiq= step option (all, or a comma list of email, meetings, files, teams, people and connectors) is parsed, refused for unknown sources (naming the known ones) and on approve steps, and taught to the plan editor (option list and round trip). all uses the copilot strategy with no capabilities, a list with connectors uses copilot with those capabilities, any other list uses grounding. The plan check needs the plan profile's Work IQ account (naming proofkin auth login workiq) and a target that is the owner's digital worker or a peer with a Microsoft 365 grant (naming the grant command); the step is marked, a peer gets at most its grant's labels, and a later step after a workiq= step on the owner's own worker gets a warning, not an error. When the step is sent, after its peer is picked, the agent searches Work IQ with the step's own words through the audited client (a call context for the run and step, so budgets apply), builds the retrieval section for that peer's audience and puts it before Your task: in the guarded prompt; the kept results' labels are the step's actual labels, which the send-time check of a later step uses. A Work IQ error or a budget refusal fails the step with its one-line message. The run record keeps per step the sources, labels, kept and withheld counts and request ids. The web UI's plan check, the plans it starts and its Work IQ import, and the agent's /plan command, read the profile's settings when they run, so a Work IQ sign-in made while the agent runs (proofkin auth login workiq in another process) counts at once.

A step whose target is @workiq is run by the plan's own agent, never sent to a peer: it calls Work IQ's ask tool through the audited client with the step's own words plus the results of the steps it runs after (capped like other steps), and agent=<id> (letters, digits and - _ . : @, at most 200 characters) is sent as agentId. Its output is the answer and its cited sources for the local audience; the step is marked as Microsoft 365 content with its citations' labels, and a citation without label information adds the label unknown, which no peers allow --m365 grant can include, so no peer gets that output (a later step on a peer without a grant, or with a narrower one, is refused). The answer reaches later steps through after, and save= writes the mark and a source note saying it was a Work IQ answer. Plan errors say an answer is context and never proof for claims=, verify=, apply=, mcp=, skill=, attempts=, levels=, team and approve on a @workiq step. The plan check needs the profile's Work IQ account. The run shows it as done by workiq (or workiq:<agent id>), with no evidence and not verified: its report heads it (Work IQ) on workiq, naming neither the plan's provider nor a peer, and says No evidence: an answer from Microsoft 365 Copilot is context, never proof (a peer's step without evidence still says the peer runs an older version). The web UI's task for it reads Step <id> · Microsoft 365 Copilot (Work IQ), or Microsoft 365 agent <id> (Work IQ) when it asks one, never the plan's provider, and its target keeps who answered it as it is (workiq:<agent id>, though the id has colons). proofkin workiq agents lists the agents list_agents returns (name and id), from structuredContent or, as Work IQ gives them, from the JSON list in the text content. The plan editor knows the @workiq target.

proofkin kb import workiq <topic> --query <text> [--from SOURCES] [--replace] runs Work IQ's retrieve through the audited client for the profile (purpose knowledge-import, the query on one line, --from taking the sources of the workiq= option with the same strategy and capabilities and the same refusals, default all), builds the retrieval section for the local audience and saves it as the topic: marked as Microsoft 365 content with the labels of the kept results (unknown for a result without label information), with the front matter lines query: and retrieved: (the date) and the source note Work IQ retrieve. An existing topic is not overwritten without --replace (and Work IQ is not asked), and when no result was kept nothing is written and the error says how many results were withheld and why. The saved topic works with context=, and its mark goes through the plan check to the steps that use it. POST /api/kb/import/workiq (topic, query, from, replace) is token-guarded, does the same and answers with the topic and the kept and withheld counts and labels.

A workiq= step's signed evidence records the Work IQ context its task had by hash, never its content: the plan's agent sends the task with where the Microsoft 365 section is in its prompt and how many results it held with their labels, and the worker refuses a task whose section isn't a whole part of its prompt, else signs context [{source workiq, sha256 of exactly that part, results, labels}] (a team step's lead too), and its result's summary says Work context from Microsoft 365 (Work IQ) with the count, labels and the start of the hash. The run record keeps the section's SHA-256, and the saved run keeps the section itself next to its run.json (<step>.workiq.md), never in it, so a run.json shared to be verified holds no Microsoft 365 content; runs verify fails a step whose evidence doesn't record the hash the run kept for it, or, given the run's folder, whose kept section no longer has its hash. Records without context sign as before; claims never rest on Work IQ content.

proofkin spec import --from <url> --profile NAME --set peer=... imports a spec in a Word (.docx), Markdown (.md, .markdown) or text (.txt) document on SharePoint or OneDrive through Work IQ, with the profile's sign-in: fetch reads the driveItem at /shares/u!<base64url of the link> (name, size, type, sensitivity label), then fetch_blob its content, each call through the audited client with purpose spec-import and the profile's budgets. A link that isn't https on *.sharepoint.com, *.sharepoint-df.com (Microsoft's own pre-production SharePoint), onedrive.live.com or 1drv.ms, or --from with a folder, is refused before any call; a statusCode other than 200 fails with Work IQ's error class; when fetch or fetch_blob answers isError, the error is Work IQ's <tool> tool reported an error for the document: <what the tool said, on one line, redacted, at most 300 characters>, ending there when it said nothing (a failure with a fix of its own, such as billing or sign-in, keeps the client's error); another type of document, or one over 4 MB, is refused before its content is fetched, and so is one whose sensitivity label has protectionEnabled true (its content is encrypted): it is refused after fetch, before fetch_blob, naming the label; the content must decode to its sizeBytes and be of a type read. A Word document is read as Markdown from word/document.xml only (at most 8 MB): Title and Heading1-6 become # to ######, list paragraphs - , tables Markdown rows, w:tab a tab and w:br a line break; headers, footers, comments and images are left out. The text is redacted and read as a Spec Kit spec.md: claims US-, FR- and SC-, or DOC-1 (a sign-off) with a warning when it has neither a user story nor a requirement. The plan names the document by its file name, its link only in the plan's comment; it is saved as knowledge topic spec-<document>, its text as external content (a workiq:document:<file name> envelope), marked origin: workiq with its sensitivity label (unknown without label information), so a peer without a grant that includes the label is refused by the plan check, and the summary names the label peers need. The implement-speckit playbook's spec takes such a link in the web UI's Plan mode.

The Work IQ commands work through the program itself, as a user runs them, against a fake Work IQ and Entra: auth login workiq --device-code signs in, workiq doctor passes its five checks, workiq agents lists the agents, kb import workiq saves what the content policy keeps (withheld counted), and an agent started with proofkin --name runs a plan's @workiq step itself and sends a workiq= step to a peer with only the results its Microsoft 365 grant allows; runs verify passes and the step's signed evidence records the context by the hash of the section the run kept; workiq usage counts every call; each run uses the refresh token the run before saved (Entra rotates them); after auth logout workiq the doctor fails. The same commands work through the Work IQ CLI given with --cli-path. The test-only settings PROOFKIN_TEST_WORKIQ_URL and PROOFKIN_TEST_ENTRA_URL that point the program at the fakes take only a root http(s) address on the loopback interface (localhost or a loopback IP); any other value is refused, never replaced by the real service, so no token goes elsewhere.

Microsoft 365 content never goes on GitHub through a tracked run (issue #250): the tracker comments each step's result, or why it failed, on its issue, and the repository may be public, so what a step that may hold Microsoft 365 content ended with stays in the run's record, and its comment says so and names the agent that has it. A step may hold it if it brings some (workiq=, @workiq), its model may read some (mcp=workiq), it is marked with some (a context= topic from Microsoft 365), its signed evidence names labels, or a step it waits for held some. Other steps' results, and a sign-off's note (its approver's own words), are posted as before. The plan editor's tracking note says so. A plan imported from a Microsoft 365 document (spec import --from, issue #261) quotes the document in its claims and steps, which a tracked run posts, so it says track: off right after its comments, after a comment saying why that names the document's sensitivity label (no label information without one): its runs aren't tracked unless the user takes that line out, and the import's summary says so. A Spec Kit or OpenSpec folder's plan has no track: line.

A live check against a real tenant's Work IQ, behind PROOFKIN_LIVE_WORKIQ=cli|hosted (scripts/live_workiq.py; python scripts/evidence.py --live runs it when that is set), only reads: a fresh profile signs in to Work IQ (through the Work IQ CLI, or with Proofkin's device code sign-in), its doctor passes every check with one retrieve, proofkin workiq agents reads the agents list Work IQ gives (only how many is shown), and its agent runs a plan whose workiq= step goes to the profile's own digital worker on real Copilot and whose @workiq step gets Microsoft 365 Copilot's answer. The run's signed evidence verifies, the step's evidence records the Work IQ context by its hash and nothing else, and every call in the profile's Work IQ audit file was a read tool. Step outputs stay out of its log and email addresses are masked. Without PROOFKIN_LIVE_WORKIQ the check is not run and fails nothing.

A folder can offer Work IQ to its owner's tasks as its MCP server workiq (proofkin mcp add <folder> workiq --workiq [--tool ...]; the name is workiq, it has no command or URL, only tools that read: retrieve, ask, fetch, search_paths, get_schema, list_agents, call_function, and any task access may use it). A task that asks for mcp=workiq gets, for that task only, http://127.0.0.1:<port>/mcp/workiq/<session> with a random bearer; the agent calls Work IQ itself through the profile's audited client, so the model's MCP config holds no token. The session lists only the allowed tools Work IQ offers, never one whose MCP annotations say it changes things (readOnlyHint false or destructiveHint true), refuses any other tool before it reaches Work IQ, puts every result through the content policy for the task's audience (a peer audience gets only retrieve and ask, within its labels), audits each call with purpose gateway, needs its bearer, refuses requests with an Origin header, and closes when the task ends. A digital worker's owner's tasks see what Work IQ allows (peers: WIQ-17). A plan marks a step with mcp=workiq, and the steps after it, with the label unknown, so nothing made from what its model read goes to a peer.

A peer's task gets Work IQ through the gateway (mcp=workiq) only when the agent's owner granted that peer --m365-tools: its session then offers only retrieve and ask, whose results carry labels, and the content policy gives it only results with the labels of its grant; every call is audited with the peer's name as its audience. Without the grant the task is refused before its model starts, and the refusal names the grant to add (proofkin peers allow <peer> --m365 <labels> --m365-tools). The grant is read again when the task starts. The requester's plan marks the step's output unknown (WIQ-16), so it goes no further to a peer.

A plan makes Microsoft 365 changes only as its owner signed them off (docs/work-iq.md section 7). A step whose changes a later @workiq apply=STEP step makes is told to propose them in one fenced m365-changes block, one JSON object a line: tool is create_entity, update_entity, delete_entity or do_action; path a Microsoft Graph path that starts with / with no host, no .. and no control characters, at most 2 KB; body a JSON object, none for a delete; ifMatch only for an update or a delete; at most 20 changes and 256 KB. A block that breaks a rule fails the step, naming the line and the rule. The approve @me step between them shows each change first (a mail's recipients, subject and first 10 lines with HTML removed; another change's verb, path and the first 500 characters of its body) and the list's SHA-256 over its canonical JSON, so the approver's signed answer (its prompt_sha256) covers exactly that list. The apply step has no model: it makes the changes only after a verified approval signed by its own agent for a request that showed the list as it is now, calls each once, in order, with exactly the proposed arguments (parentUrl, entityUrl or actionUrl, jsonBody, and If-Match), and stops at the first that fails or whose outcome is unknown; its result lists each outcome (done, accepted for a 202, failed, outcome unknown) and the changes not made. A 4xx status in the answer is failed, with the classified error and fix. A status of 500 or more leaves the outcome unknown and says to check in Microsoft 365 before trying again. This applies even when Work IQ did not flag the call as an error. A rejected sign-off makes none. The plan check refuses an apply step, naming the fix, without an approve @me between the two steps (a peer's sign-off doesn't count), when it doesn't run after the step, when another step applies the same step, with an option that would make it more than that, or when the profile doesn't allow changes (proofkin workiq changes on sets workiq_changes in profile.json; off by default; workiq doctor and the Work IQ card say which). Neither step's result goes on GitHub.

A digital worker's task for its owner with mcp=workiq (the gateway's Local audience; never a plan step's task, whose origin names a step, nor a peer's, whatever its grant) may change Microsoft 365 while the owner is there to answer (docs/work-iq.md sections 6 and 7), only when the profile whose Work IQ account it uses allows changes (proofkin workiq changes on [--wait 5m]: a sign-off waits 1 to 10 minutes, given as 5m or 5, 5 by default) and the folder's workiq server does too (proofkin mcp add <folder> workiq --workiq --changes; --changes is only for --workiq, --tool may also name the change tools, and mcp list shows changes). Its session then lists Work IQ's change tools create_entity, update_entity, delete_entity and do_action, though their annotations say they change things; otherwise they aren't listed, and a call is refused before any sign-off or Work IQ call. It lists them without Work IQ's optional sessionId and agentId in each one's inputSchema (its properties and required), so the model isn't asked for them; the read tools' schemas are listed as Work IQ gives them. A change call takes parentUrl, entityUrl or actionUrl, jsonBody and headers (If-Match); a sessionId (a string: Work IQ's telemetry ID) and an agentId that is null or absent are accepted and left out of the change, so they aren't signed off, shown in the sign-off or sent to Work IQ, and an agentId that isn't null is refused before any sign-off, saying that a change can't name a Work IQ agent. A change call is held to the rules of a plan's changes (one that breaks a rule gets a tool error naming it, and nobody is asked), then becomes a signed approval request from the worker to its owner's agent, titled Microsoft 365 change from <worker>, whose text shows the change as a plan's sign-off shows one, its SHA-256 and its task (the owner's task number when it has one, and the first 200 characters of its prompt); the call waits for the answer up to the wait, in awake time. Only a verified approval signed by the owner, for exactly that text, makes the change, once, with exactly the call's arguments but sessionId and agentId (a jsonBody given as a JSON string is sent as the object it encodes), and the model gets how it ended: done, with a created entity's id and link; accepted, for a 202; failed; or outcome unknown. A 4xx answer is failed, and an answer with a status of 500 or more is of unknown outcome and says to check in Microsoft 365 before trying again. Both are tool errors for the model (isError: true) and the changes list records the same outcome, even when Work IQ did not flag the call as an error. A rejection or a request for changes sends nothing, and the model gets the owner's note; with no answer in time the request is withdrawn from the owner's agent, so a late answer finds none and makes nothing. The same call again is a sign-off of its own. With change tools the session's server gets a tool timeout of the wait plus 60 seconds, in milliseconds, in Copilot's config and in the bridge's JSON for Claude; without them it has none. Each change is audited as a gateway call with its path's SHA-256, and the task's signed result ends with a Microsoft 365 changes this task made section naming each change's verb, path and outcome, never its body. workiq doctor and the web UI's Work IQ card say whether changes are on and how long a sign-off waits.

A sign-off that waits for its owner can also be told in Microsoft 365, so the owner needn't watch the web UI; they still answer it in Proofkin (docs/work-iq.md section 7). Off by default, the owner opts in once per profile: proofkin workiq notices mail sets workiq_notices {"to": "mail"} in profile.json, mail to the signed-in account's own address (its UPN); proofkin workiq notices teams --chat <id> sets {"to": "teams", "chat": "<id>"} only once a fetch of /me/chats/{id}?$select=id,topic,chatType says the account is a member of the chat (one it isn't a member of is refused and not kept); proofkin workiq notices teams --list shows the account's recent chats (a fetch of /me/chats?$select=id,topic,chatType&$top=20) and keeps nothing; Teams' chat with yourself (48:notes) is neither listed nor taken; proofkin workiq notices off removes the setting. Those reads are audited as the command's own. A digital worker that uses its owner's Work IQ uses its owner's setting and account, so its owner gets the notice, and workiq notices is refused for it. workiq doctor and the web UI's Work IQ card (GET /api/workiq's notices and notices_line) say where notices go. One notice is sent for each sign-off that waits for the owner: a plan's approve @me step (titled Plan step <id>, with its run and step), including one that shows Microsoft 365 changes, and a change a digital worker's task holds for its owner (with the owner's task number). By mail it is one do_action on /me/sendMail with the subject Proofkin: sign-off waiting: <title>, the text as Text, the account's own address as its only recipient and saveToSentItems false; in Teams it is one create_entity on /chats/{id}/messages with the text as text. The text says <agent> waits for your sign-off of "<title>" (run <run id>, step <step>), to answer it in Proofkin's web UI or with /approve in the agent's terminal, and that it holds nothing of what is signed off: never a change's content, recipients or body, nor any step's result. The title is cut to 200 characters, redacted and stripped of control and invisible formatting characters. A notice is a change Proofkin makes with the account, which the owner opted in to, so it needs no sign-off of its own: it goes through the audited client with purpose notice, counted against the budgets, and is sent once, in the background, and never again. The sign-off waits as it would without it (a held change's wait runs from when the call was held). A notice whose call Work IQ fails or refuses is told in the activity and recorded in the audit. A notice that can't be sent at all (no usable Work IQ account, an account address that isn't an email address, a chat id that isn't one) makes no call, so it is told in the activity only. Either way, the sign-off still waits and is answered as usual.

call_function is one of the gateway's read tools (Work IQ CLI 1.0.1 annotates it read only): a folder's workiq server offers it to its owner's own tasks unless --tool names fewer, and like fetch, whose results carry no sensitivity labels, it never goes to a peer's task, even one granted --m365-tools (those get only retrieve and ask). Like any tool, it is refused if its annotations say it changes things.

A workiq= step or kb import workiq whose copilot retrieve reports the generic tool error An error occurred invoking 'retrieve' (kind Tool and class Tool) searches once more with grounding for the same query and audience, omitting GraphConnectors. For all, grounding uses Email, Meetings, OneDriveAndSharePoint, TeamsMessages and People; a list keeps only its named sources other than connectors. Connectors alone, a search already using grounding, any other error text or class, and models' gateway calls do not use this fallback. Both calls go through the audited client and count against the budgets. The step's progress and its saved Work IQ sources (runs show and the web UI) say when the search fell back without connectors, as does the import. The grounding results follow the usual content policy. If grounding fails too, its error says that the copilot search failed first.

Importing Microsoft's Work IQ plugin (the shape of microsoft/work-iq:plugins/workiq: .github/plugin/plugin.json, skills/, and a .mcp.json whose server is the hosted https://workiq.svc.cloud.microsoft/mcp with oauthClientId) keeps its skills and makes its MCP server a Work IQ template: its own connection and sign-in settings are dropped, the review notes that it is offered through this agent's own Work IQ sign-in and gateway with only its tools that read, and offering it in a folder gives the agent's workiq server (no URL, command or headers; it must be named workiq). The Work IQ CLI's server (npx @microsoft/workiq mcp, or workiq mcp) is recognized the same way; other servers are not.

The web UI has a token-guarded API for the profile's Work IQ account, which reads the profile as its files are now, so a sign-in made in another process counts. GET /api/workiq answers whether the account the agent uses is signed in, its line, how it connects (hosted or cli), its user, the CLI's account and path for a CLI account, the profile it belongs to (a digital worker may use its owner's) and whether that is this profile, why a digital worker its owner didn't let use theirs has none (not_used), the sign-in command, whether this profile allows Microsoft 365 changes (changes, see WIQ-18), and today's calls against the per-day and per-run budgets (with each run's calls). POST /api/workiq/doctor answers the doctor's checks with their results, details and fixes, always as 200. POST /api/workiq/sign-in (account, cli_path) signs the profile in through Microsoft's Work IQ CLI as proofkin auth login workiq --cli does and answers who signed in and the line; DELETE /api/workiq signs out, and is refused when not signed in; each adds a line to the activity. PUT /api/workiq/budget (per_day, per_run) sets the budgets. Errors are 400s in the sign-in's or set_budget's own words. A digital worker that uses its owner's account sees it but is refused signing in, signing out and budgets: its owner does those. The page's Work IQ card, after the GitHub card, shows this from GET /api/workiq and acts through these endpoints; every element its script looks up is on the page, and its sign-in and budget dialogs close with Escape and Cancel like the others.

The web UI sets, changes and removes a peer's Microsoft 365 grant (labels, Work IQ tools) with the CLI's rules, and shows it. POST /api/trust and PUT /api/trust/{id} take m365 as proofkin peers allow takes --m365 and --m365-tools: left out, a change keeps the peer's grant and adding a peer again keeps the grant of the entry it replaces (else none); null gives no grant (like --m365 off); {labels, tools} gives that grant, built by M365Grant::from_labels from label names only, so it needs at least one label, never takes unknown or off (off isn't read as --m365 off, alone or among other labels, with tools or without: null is how a peer gets no grant) and keeps each label once whatever its case. A grant it refuses is a 400 that says what is wrong in the dialog's words, without the CLI's flags (The labels can't include 'unknown': it stands for content with no label information, whose sensitivity isn't known, so no peer gets it; Give at least one label name, e.g. General, Public, unlabeled), and leaves the peer's entry as it was. peers.json has the grant after each change, the allowlist in /api/state shows it (labels and tools, or null) and the change's activity line says it (Microsoft 365: General, Public, and that its tasks may use Work IQ). The allowlist dialog, for Add peer and Change…, offers it after the folders: a checkbox to let the peer receive Microsoft 365 content, the sensitivity labels it may receive, comma separated (unlabeled allows content with no label; content without label information never goes to a peer), and a checkbox to let its tasks use this agent's Work IQ, read only; Change… fills them from the peer's grant and sends null when the first is cleared, and every element the page's script looks up for them is in the dialog. The peers list shows a granted peer's grant (M365: General, Public · Work IQ tools). The plan builder offers workiq= and @workiq with the agents Work IQ lists. A step that goes to a peer or squad (not a sign-off or @workiq step; a team step only when its text has workiq=, to clear it) has a Microsoft 365 (Work IQ) group in its options with a checkbox per source (all, email, meetings, files, teams, people, connectors; all clears the others and another source clears all) that sets its workiq= values, with a hint that the step searches Microsoft 365 for its own words when it is sent and a peer gets only what its grant allows. Who runs a step can be Microsoft 365 Copilot (@workiq): choosing it takes out the folder, provider and the options such a step can't have (checks, claims, retries, patch, MCP servers, skills, knowledge, levels, model, effort, base, workiq=), agent= goes when a step moves to or from @workiq, and the step gets an optional Agent select filled from GET /api/workiq/agents, which sets agent=<id>. That route answers {agents: [{name, id}]}, the declarative agents Work IQ lists for the account the profile uses, only with the access token; not signed in, or a Work IQ error, is a 400 with its message on one line, which the select shows as its hint. A plan with workiq=email,files or @workiq agent=x reads into the builder as it is, and editing those options changes only them in the plan text. The editor's palette has workiq=all and each source as chips under Checks and MCP servers, each titled with what it searches. The Knowledge section has Import from Microsoft 365: a dialog with the topic name, what to look for, where to look (the sources of workiq=, all by default) and Replace the topic if it exists, which says the topic keeps where it came from (Microsoft 365, with the labels of what it kept), so it goes only to peers whose grant covers them. It closes with Escape and Cancel, every element the page's script looks up for it is in it, and it sends {topic, query, from, replace} to POST /api/kb/import/workiq: it then shows the topic, how many results were kept with their labels and how many were withheld, or the route's error in its words as a sentence (starting with a capital), and loads the knowledge list again (GET /api/ops lists the topic with its labels). The Knowledge list shows such a topic's labels on its line (Microsoft 365 · General, no label information; a mark without labels reads unlabeled), titled with who it may go to: only peers whose Microsoft 365 grant covers them, or no peer when it has content without label information. GET /api/runs/{id} answers workiq: for each step that used Work IQ (its workiq= search, or a @workiq step's answer), in step order, its sources (title, kind, label, link), labels and how many results were kept and withheld, never the context itself, which stays in the run's folder; steps without one have no entry.       The run dialog shows them per step, between the run's work and its report: Microsoft 365: 2 results kept (General), 1 withheld, and each source as plain text, a link only when it is a web address. The page never shows the internal label unknown: in the run dialog's counts and sources and the import's result it says no label information (1 result kept (no label information), none withheld, for an answer without citations).

Every task result names the model that did the work, as its provider says: Copilot from the CLI's usage events of the session's own agent (else the model the task asked for), Claude from the Agent SDK's init message, Codex from the thread's model or the top-level model of the profile's own config.toml. A worker sends it with the result (a field older peers ignore) and names it in the signed output's evidence summary, so the record vouches for it and older requesters verify it as before; names are cleaned to the characters model names use before they are shown. The web UI's task and step cards (after the provider), the worker's audit log, run records and reports, the tracker's step comments and the CLI's printed results show it; without a model the result is as before.

claims.claim: A profile's owner sets each provider's default model and the models tasks may ask for (proofkin models default <provider> <model>|none and models allow <provider> <list>|any), kept in profile.json and left out when unset. A default must be allowed; with a list and no default, tasks that name none run on the first in the list. models list prints the models Copilot offers the account and marks the default and the allowed ones. A task that names no model runs on the default, an agent's executor limits Copilot sessions to the list, and its hello tells peers the defaults and lists of the providers it serves (older peers' hellos read as saying nothing), cleaned of malformed names. An agent definition's model: is kept (inherit and names that aren't model names are left out).

A task chooses its model: a plan step's model= option (given once, a model's name, not on sign-offs, team steps or @workiq steps; a step with agent= and no model= takes the agent's model), /ask and /delegate --model right after the target, the web UI's Run task form (a Model list of what the chosen peer or this agent lets you pick, see MDL-10) and the model argument of the MCP and A2A delegate; the plan editor and builder read and write model=. The step's task carries it, the plan check warns when every peer a step may go to says it doesn't allow the model, the worker refuses a task asking for a model its owner doesn't allow (a refusal naming the allowed ones) and runs an allowed one, and the result, get_task and the A2A metadata name the model that did the work.

The allowlist changes what a peer may do in place (Change…: whether it may delegate, its hourly limit, its access level and its folders), keeping its name and addresses, and its Microsoft 365 grant unless the change sets it (WIQ-23): saved to peers.json and applied at once, a connected peer stays connected and learns its folders; a folder this agent doesn't share, or a peer that isn't on the allowlist, is refused. Chat only says what it means when hovered.

A task on its own can go to a squad (the web UI's Run on lists squads with an online member serving the provider, /delegate <provider>@#squad, the MCP and A2A delegate with peer #squad): its least busy member that can run it, as a plan step on the squad would, moving to another member while one turns it down or goes away before running it; its card names the member and the squad. A squad that doesn't exist, or that no member can run the task for, is refused with the reason.

A squad step or task that names a model goes to a member that allows it (as the members' hellos say; one that says nothing allows any), even when another member is less busy; if none does, it goes to the least busy as before, which refuses it saying why.

Squads are changed in place (the web UI's Change… on a squad, its name fixed; proofkin squad create replaces one), and New squad refuses a name that is taken; members that left the allowlist are listed so they can be dropped. Bad squad and member names are refused in words about squads and peers.

The squad dialog says what each peer would take as a member: whose digital worker it is and its role, the providers it runs with their default model and reasoning, and the folders it shares (marked when they have a team plan); an offline one says that shows when it connects. A peer that runs no providers and leads no team plan (an agent that only delegates), or shares no folder, takes no squad steps, as the plan check says (sign-offs need a person): the dialog and the squads card say so and why, the card warns when no online member can take its steps, and a squad whose members all take none isn't saved.

The GitHub card says where each task branch's work is, from one GraphQL query for all of a repository's branches, checked against the repository's branch as GitHub has it (fetched when the clone's last fetch is over 5 minutes old; when it can't be, the card says the states are as of the last fetch): its newest pull request (open, merged or closed, and whether it has the branch as it is), its commit or its changes (the same content in every file it changes) on the repository's branch already, the issues it is for all closed (and the pull requests from other branches that closed them, named on the card, in Review changes and in the delete confirmation as possibly having its work), and its commits, files and lines that aren't there. A branch is safe to delete only when its work is on the repository's branch or a pull request merged it as it is: closed issues, a closed pull request, or one that merged an earlier version of it don't make it safe. The card offers only Delete branch then, as nothing is left to review (on GitHub first, then in the clone, only p2p/ branches); Review changes and Delete branch, its confirmation saying what is lost, once its pull request was closed as it is or its issues are all closed (it isn't proposed again); Review changes and Open PR while there is work to merge and no pull request is open; and Review changes alone while one is open. It says how many older branches it doesn't show.

Review changes on a task branch (GET /api/repos/NAME/changes?branch=, only p2p/ branches of a linked repository) shows what a pull request from it would carry before it is opened or the branch deleted: its commits that aren't on the repository's branch (up to 50), the proof the pull request would carry, the files it changes with lines added and removed (binary files say so), and the diff from where the branches split, cut at 400 KB on a line's end and saying so; each file's lines read by its hunks' counts, shown as text (never markup). The pull request form says what it would change, with a link back to the review.

A pull request a plan's pull request step opens lists the plan's sign-offs before it: each approval step it comes after, with who approved it, their agent's key, when, and their note as code (so it mentions no one and links nothing), from the record the approver's agent signed. The folder's agent lists only approvals that verify for exactly their words and were asked for by the peer that asks for the pull request, says how many it left out, and names the evidence run that has them (proofkin runs verify).

A pull request step asks the people who signed off before it to review the pull request it opens, by GitHub account: the profile's own (its GitHub sign-in) for the owner's sign-offs, and for a peer's, the account the allowlist has for it (peers allow --github, peers github, or the web UI's allowlist dialog; kept when the peer is allowed again, empty forgets it). reviewers= names others instead (me, an allowlisted peer, or a GitHub login, each once, at most 10; none asks no one; only on pull request steps), and the plan check warns about each one whose account it doesn't know, saying how to set it. The folder's agent asks GitHub for each one separately when it opens the pull request (never again for one it opened before), doesn't ask its own account (the author), and its signed result says who was asked, and who wasn't and why.

A folder that takes pull request steps can have its owner approve each one (share pull-requests --approve, or Ask me to approve each one in the web UI; peers learn that it does): the request waits in the owner's approvals saying who asks, the title, branch and commit, the sign-offs, reviewers and issues; nothing is pushed or opened until they approve, a rejection fails the step with their reason, the pull request says they approved it with their note, and one an earlier try opened isn't asked about again. A finished run's card lists the work a pull request can be opened from (each signed commit a model's step made in a peer's folder that no other step of the run builds on, unless a pull request step of the run saw it merged) and why it can't be now; Open pull request (POST /api/runs/ID/pull-request with a title and reviewers) sends the folder's agent the ask with the run's sign-offs on that work and the reviewers resolved as reviewers= does, and the pull request says who asked for it from which evidence run.

A task in a linked repository's folder starts from the repository's latest commit: before it starts, its agent fetches the repository's branch (unless the clone fetched it in the last minute) and fast-forwards the clone, telling the requester (updated folder 'app' to its repository's latest commit abc1234 (N newer commits)). The clone is left as it is when the repository can't be reached, it has another branch checked out, its branch has commits the repository's hasn't, or the update would overwrite its local changes; the task then starts from the clone's commit and its result says which one and why.

A sign-off's approver can ask for changes instead of approving or rejecting (web UI Ask for changes, terminal /changes N WHAT, POST /api/approvals/ID with changes and a note; signed as not approved, saying so) while the sign-off allows another round (changes=N on it, 0 to 5, default 2; only sign-offs take it): the steps a model did that it waits for directly are done again, each from its own earlier commit with the note, their cards saying so, then the sign-off asks again with the new results and the note it answered. A request that doesn't offer it refuses it, and asking for changes needs a note.

A plan's step can start from an earlier evidence run's work, merged or not (base=RUN:STEP; only on steps a model does in a folder, not with apply=): the commit step STEP of run RUN made, read from the run's signed record, which must check out (signatures and the patch's signed hash), is applied in its worktree first. The plan check says when the run, the step or its work isn't there, the step fails saying so if it is gone by then, and the run's report says which run's work the step started from. A run's card offers Build on it, which starts such a plan.

A task that asks for its folder's checks gives its model (Copilot or Claude; not Codex, which takes no MCP servers) a run_check tool: the worker starts proofkin task-checks as the task's MCP server proofkin-checks, which runs one of the step's checks in the task's workspace, outside the model's sandbox as the runtime does, and answers whether it passed, with its exit code, time and the end of its output (secrets redacted), at most 10 runs a task, each up to 20 minutes. A check the step doesn't name is refused, and so is an 11th run. The runtime still runs the checks after the model, and only those runs are evidence.

A model run that stops before it finishes (it runs out of time, a Copilot run being allowed up to an hour of awake time (NET-8), or its provider fails) is a failed attempt: with attempts left, the next one goes on in the same worktree, told why the last run stopped, its progress saying it goes on from where the last run stopped and the result listing the stopped attempt; when it was the last attempt, what the model changed is committed to the task's branch before the error goes back, naming the branch and commit. A step whose task failed shows its peer's error alone: only a result that says it succeeded without the record its checks or sign-off need is suspect.

A task that stops before its work is committed other than by its model's run stopping (it is cancelled, or its agent stops) keeps what the model changed (issue #243): its worktree, asked to when the task made it, commits what is left to the task's branch as "<subject> (unfinished)" when it goes, leaving out build and tool caches as task commits do. A worktree that wasn't asked to (one that checks a patch) commits nothing, and once a task's work was committed nothing more is.

With a tracker linked, Plan mode and the plan editor offer Track on GitHub beside Run plan: a new issue (with a sub-issue per step), an existing issue it works on (by number) or don't track, which reads and writes the plan's track: line (a title, #N or N, off in any case; a track: line in a step's text isn't the plan's). The line under it says what running the plan does there before it runs: the repository and the board (links that open a new tab), the account the issues are assigned to, the new issue's title when the plan names one, and that anyone can read them when the repository is public (the tracker reads its visibility; tracker status says it too), or that nothing goes to GitHub. An existing issue is looked up as its number is typed (GET /api/tracker/issues/N): its title, with a warning when it is closed (running reopens it), doesn't exist (the plan would run untracked) or can't be looked up; Run plan and Schedule… ask for the number when it is missing instead of opening a new issue.

The Health card's summary counts evidence runs as passed, failed and without claims (a run without claims proves nothing, so it neither passed nor failed), leaves out counts that are zero, and shows times as durations.

A plan can set model: and effort: once each for its model steps. A step's own model= or effort= wins; sign-off, pull request, team and @workiq steps don't inherit either. The parser refuses duplicate or invalid settings and a model: line with mixed providers. The check warns when a step would be refused or when no step uses a setting. In Plan mode and the editor, labeled Model and Reasoning choices read and write those lines beside Run plan. The model menu offers what the steps' peers allow in common and names their shared default; only reasoning is selectable with mixed providers. The Builder keeps the lines and names the inherited choices, and each dispatched task and signed result use the effective settings.

A task works at a reasoning effort (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh or max): the one it asks for (a plan step's effort=, given once and not on sign-offs, team steps or @workiq steps; /ask and /delegate --effort with --model in either order; the web UI's Reasoning field; the MCP and A2A delegate's effort), else the profile's default for the provider (proofkin models effort, or models default --effort), which peers learn from the hello (a hello without one reads as none). The worker refuses a name that isn't an effort, and one its owner doesn't allow (MDL-7). Copilot gets it fitted to what the task's model supports (the nearest it supports below the one asked for, none if it supports none, and the task runs at the model's own if the CLI refuses it); Claude gets low to max (minimal is low) and Codex all of them, through the bridge. The result names the model with its effort, e.g. claude-opus-5.5 (max reasoning), in characters every version of Proofkin shows as they are, and so do the signed output, the audit log and the CLI; models list shows the efforts each Copilot model supports.

Wherever a model is chosen, the default model and reasoning effort are the selected choice, named when the agent that runs the task says them: the Run task form's Model list (the default, then what the chosen peer or this agent lets you pick, see MDL-10; with Any peer or a squad, each peer's default) and Reasoning list (the default effort as the chosen model takes it, then the levels it allows that the model supports), and the plan builder's Model and Reasoning fields for the step's peer. The This agent card lists the model and effort each provider's tasks run at, and the models and efforts peers may ask for; a boss that only delegates lists what its digital workers run.

A digital worker runs on its owner's model settings (default model, allowed models, reasoning effort and allowed efforts) for each provider it sets nothing for, as it runs on its owner's accounts: its agent, its executor, its hello and the web UI use them, and a running worker follows them when they change (MDL-8), and proofkin models list says which are its owner's; a provider it sets anything for runs on its own setting.

A step that names an issue (issue=#N) on a tracked run gets the issue's title and body, as its tracker has them, in front of its task as external content (Proofkin's own markers left out, secrets redacted, cut at 20,000 characters saying how much was left out and where the whole issue is; after the earlier steps' results), so the plan needn't repeat them and the model needn't look them up; a sign-off shows them to the person. Its commit is titled with the issue's title, the step's own first line under it. Steps that name no issue get none.

Putting issues on the board (Add existing issues, tracker add, and a tracked run's issues) holds when GitHub answers a batch of adds with an error: each add that fails is looked up on the board first, as GitHub may have carried it out (an HTTP 502 for a batch it did) or put it there itself (a board's Auto-add sub-issues workflow adds a run's sub-issues when the run's issue goes on it, and adding them then says "Content already exists in this project"); those still missing are added again, five to a request, and only what still fails is a problem, once. Every item it added gets its status (and a run's items their agent). Queries GitHub answers with a 502, 503 or 504 are asked again, twice at most; mutations never are.

A profile's owner chooses the reasoning efforts tasks may ask a provider for (proofkin models allow <provider> --efforts <levels>|any, with or without models; the web UI's Models dialog), kept least to most in profile.json (all six is any, and left out). The default effort must be one of them, and the list keep it. A task asking for another is refused before it runs, naming the allowed ones; one asking for none works at the default, else the least allowed. Peers learn the list from the hello (a hello without one reads as any), cleaned of names that aren't efforts; a squad step with effort= goes first to members that allow it, and the plan check warns when every peer the step may go to says it doesn't.

claims.claim: The web UI's Models dialog (Models… on the This agent card, and on each digital worker) lists the models the account offers, by vendor, to allow any or only those ticked (named for a provider that lists none), the reasoning levels to allow, and the defaults. Saving checks the settings as a whole (the defaults must be allowed; a provider the agent doesn't run, or an agent that isn't one of its digital workers, is refused and nothing is saved), writes profile.json and applies them at once: this agent's tasks and peers use them, and a digital worker uses its own or, again, its owner's. An agent that only delegates lists the models for its digital workers with a Copilot CLI started for the purpose.

The Run task form and the plan builder list what the chosen peer lets you pick: the models it allows, else all its account offers (by vendor, with their cost multiplier; a name typed by hand only for a peer that lists none), and the reasoning levels it allows that the chosen model supports, its defaults selected (the default level as the model takes it; a model without levels says so), the levels changing with the model. For Any peer or a squad they list what their peers allow together, and an Any peer task that names a model or an effort goes to a peer that allows them.

An agent blueprint (proofkin.agent-blueprint/v1) is checked against the profile it is for: its skills, knowledge topics, folders with their checks and MCP servers, the providers it is signed in to, the models and efforts it allows, approvers on its allowlist and unique requirement ids, and a name nothing else has. Each problem has a stable code, is an error or a warning, and says what is wrong, how to fix it and the JSON pointer of the field. Asking for more than it needs (full access with no check, every tool of a server, every Work IQ source, delegation, instructions that ask for tools) is a least-privilege warning naming the narrower choice (AC-6).

A task records the usage its provider reported: the Copilot session's tokens and premium requests, the Claude Agent SDK's tokens and cost estimate, and the tokens of Codex's turn. A provider that reports none records none, not zero. Usage adds up over a task's attempts, goes back to the requester with the result (older peers ignore it) and is kept in the worker's audit entry, which holds no prompt or output text. The web UI shows it on a finished task and in the audit, and proofkin audit sums it per peer and provider.

claims.claim: The profile's factory keeps drafts, and each agent's lifecycle state and history (who, when, what), in its factory folder: written atomically under a lock, for its owner only. They survive restarts and concurrent writers, a damaged file is reported with its path and left as it is, a name has one agent, and an agent with releases is never deleted. proofkin factory list, show, edit, check and delete work on them: edit takes the blueprint from an editor, a file or stdin and keeps it with its problems (text that isn't JSON or renames the agent isn't saved), and check fails while a draft has errors, showing each with its fix.

An agent's eval suite has cases that each name the requirement they prove, give a task, its fixtures and what to expect, and every requirement needs a case with a deterministic expectation (AC-10). contains, not-contains, regex, json-schema, max-words, files-changed and check expectations pass and fail as the design says (check runs the folder's check in the run's folder), and a failing run's note names the expectation it missed (e.g. expected no "Not found" (not-contains), but the answer has it); a judge rubric is scored by a model, never graded here. Fixtures must be files in the agent's fixtures folder, reached without links.

proofkin factory templates lists the built-in templates with their purpose, most access and number of eval cases. Each passes validation unchanged with a case for every requirement, and proofkin factory new --template makes a draft from one with no model, on the providers the profile is signed in to (AC-4).

proofkin factory new --describe has the profile's default model write a draft from the owner's words: read-only, in an empty folder, given what the profile has as data and the description with secrets redacted. The draft is checked, and its problems go back to the model, at most 3 tries in all; then the owner gets the last draft with its problems (AC-1, AC-2). Its provenance records the provider, model, effort, template, the SHA-256 of the description (not its text), the time and the tries. Drafting grants nothing, whatever the description says (AC-3, TM-1), and needs a provider the profile is signed in to.

claims.claim: proofkin factory build turns a draft without errors into the files an agent is made of: its agent file (front matter with its name, purpose, skills and MCP servers, never tools or a model; then its instructions, the requirements its answers must meet and the rules every factory agent follows, a request outside its purpose answered with one OUT_OF_SCOPE line), its blueprint, its eval suite, the skills it follows under its own names and its team plan, which must be a valid team plan and needs delegation. The same blueprint builds the same bytes on every platform (keys sorted, LF line endings), and changing any field changes the build's hash, the SHA-256 of its files' sha256sum listing. A build is kept once by its hash, written whole, and checked against its hash whenever it is read: one changed after it was built is refused. proofkin factory show lists an agent's builds.

claims.claim: What a blueprint asks for is resolved against what its owner offers in each folder it is deployed to (proofkin factory check, its deploy folders or --folders): its tasks get at most the folder's access, the MCP servers it offers to tasks with that access, with the tools asked for, and the checks it has. What isn't offered is an error naming the command that offers it (share add keeping the folder's checks and worktrees, mcp add, mcp resume, plugin enable), and a server that offers fewer tools than every tool asked for is a warning. Resolving never shares a folder, offers a server or grants a peer anything: the shares and the allowlist are byte-identical after it (AC-5). What one blueprint asks for beyond another (more access, servers or tools, checks, Microsoft 365 sources, delegation, a new or changed team plan) is listed, for a release's sign-off.

An agent is evaluated on its blueprint's candidate models, else on its providers' defaults in the profile's model settings. A candidate is left out, with the reason, when the profile isn't signed in to its provider or doesn't allow its model or effort, the account doesn't offer it or its policy disables it, it is over max_multiplier or has no multiplier, it can't use the MCP servers the agent needs (Codex), or the agent's Microsoft 365 content would go outside the owner's own workers; proofkin factory show lists both. Among the candidates an evaluation passed, the recommendation follows the blueprint's prefer (cost, latency or quality; what isn't known counts as worst, and ties go to the first listed), and pinning it gives the model settings that keep a deployment's tasks to the models that passed.

A digital worker's memory (proofkin worker memory) puts its context topics, copied with their Microsoft 365 marks from its owner's knowledge, in front of every task it serves, as external content, at most 24,000 characters; a marked topic only for a requester who may have its labels (its owner, known by its endpoint id, or a peer whose grant names them). The task's signed output records that knowledge by hash, and its evidence the labels of marked knowledge, never its text; the requester marks what it does with the result with them: a later step goes only to a peer granted them (one done again for a sign-off too), what it saves is marked, a mark without labels still counts as unlabeled, and a lead's team results go back only to a requester who may have what any of its steps held (their evidence, failed steps included, and the lead's own Microsoft 365 content), their labels in its evidence (AC-30). Each task names the labels of what it holds, which its worker's evidence repeats. A task whose checks passed adds a lesson to the worker's lessons topic, once, capped, marked with the labels of what the task was given (unknown if its model read Work IQ itself); one whose checks failed adds none, and lessons older than the retention are removed (AC-31).
